Conjugate Heat Transfer Credibility Assessment
SiC Inverter Module Cold Plate — EV Traction Drive

1. Background and Intended Use

This report summarizes the credibility assessment for a conjugate heat transfer model of a liquid-cooled power electronics module used in a 400 V EV traction inverter. The model predicts peak die junction temperature and baseplate temperature gradients under steady operating points for design screening and margin assessment. The analysis covers single-phase coolant flow through a serpentine microchannel cold plate bonded to a copper baseplate; heat is generated by twelve 1.2 kV SiC MOSFET dies mounted on metallized DBC (AlN) with a graphite-based TIM to the baseplate.

Intended use:
- Predict the 99th-percentile junction temperature (Tj,max) for operating points within:
  - Coolant inlet temperature: 20–50 C
  - Module-level coolant flow rate: 0.8–1.6 L/min
  - Electrical losses per die: 30–95 W (thermal map provided by the controls team)
- Use in design decisions to ensure a 15 K thermal margin to the datasheet limit of 175 C for Tj during steady operating points.
- Exclusions: startup warm-up transients <15 s; two-phase regimes; off-design coolants (glycol fractions outside 30–50% vol).

2. Decision Context and Acceptance Criteria

Consequences of decision error: If the model underestimates Tj,max by more than 10 K in production conditions, there is risk of reduced lifetime or, in extreme cases, derating events in vehicle operation. The project team rated consequence as “moderate” (localized reliability, not immediate safety). Accordingly, the credibility goal is “medium-high”: we seek evidence showing expected absolute error in Tj,max ≤5 K across the stated envelope and a conservative 95% upper bound ≤10 K after accounting for input and numerical uncertainty.

Acceptance criteria for this assessment:
- Agreement with lab data across at least 80% of the intended envelope; absolute error in Tj,max ≤5 K mean and ≤10 K worst case; no systematic bias >3 K.
- Numerical errors bounded: mesh-induced uncertainty <3% on Tj,max; iterative imbalances <0.1% of heat input; energy balance closure within 0.5%.
- Inputs traceable and controlled; key uncertainties propagated through the model with quantitative impact estimates.
- Process discipline: reproducibility (configuration-managed cases and scripts), peer review, and environmental traceability.

3. System Description and Modeling Approach

Geometry and materials:
- Cold plate: Al 6061 body with a 1.2 mm deep, 0.8 mm wide serpentine microchannel, cover brazed to a copper baseplate (C11000) 4 mm thick.
- DBC: AlN 0.63 mm, Cu 0.3 mm top/bottom.
- TIM: graphite-based pad with nominal thickness 75 µm and apparent through-plane conductivity 6 W/m-K (per vendor datasheet).
- Twelve SiC dies (6 mm × 6 mm, 0.25 mm thick) with measured power maps (nonuniform).

Physics and numerics:
- Software: Ansys Fluent 2024 R1, double precision, steady segregated solver, second-order discretization for momentum and energy; pressure-velocity coupling via coupled scheme.
- Turbulence: Based on Reynolds numbers in the serpentine (Re = 850–1600 over the envelope), we used the transitional SST model with turbulence intensity at inlet set to 5% (measured on the bench) and y+ < 1 at walls. Cases at Re < 1000 were also run laminar to confirm insensitivity to model type.
- Conjugate heat transfer: Solid–fluid coupling with shared interfaces; temperature-dependent properties for water–ethylene glycol (40% vol) via ASHRAE tables; metal conductivities temperature-dependent (Cu and Al).
- Boundary conditions: Coolant inlet mass flow rate (0.8–1.6 L/min) with uniform velocity profile and measured temperature; outlet static pressure 0 Pa gauge; die heat fluxes matched to electrical losses with 98% of power dissipated as heat; 2% allocated to ambient radiation from top copper (emissivity 0.3).
- Contact representations: TIM as a homogenized layer; no additional contact resistances assumed except a calibrated multiplier discussed in Section 7.

Monitors and stopping criteria:
- Equations residuals reduced below 1e-6 (scaled) for continuity, momentum, and energy; conservation check of total heat input vs advected + radiated heat mismatch ≤0.5%; monitor stabilization of Tj,max within 0.1 K over 500 iterations.

4. Solver Correctness Checks

Before full-geometry runs, we performed targeted checks to reduce the risk of solver setup errors:

- Conduction “patch” check: A 50 mm copper plate with uniform heat flux and adiabatic sides was solved and compared to the 1D analytical temperature rise. Error in centerline temperature rise was 0.3% with second-order differencing.

- Convective benchmark: Straight microchannel (0.8 × 1.2 mm) under fully developed laminar flow with constant wall heat flux was compared against the Shah–London correlation for Nusselt number; predicted average Nusselt deviated by 1.9% at Re = 900, Pr = 4.8.

- Thermal coupling consistency: Two-domain (fluid–solid) slab test with matched grids assessed interface continuity; maximum interface temperature jump <0.02 K at 10 W/cm2.

- Energy budget: For the inverter module at a nominal point (Qtotal = 720 W), the difference between input electrical power converted to heat and the sum of coolant enthalpy rise plus radiation was 0.29%.

- Grid imprint leak test: Artificially coarsened mesh at the fluid–solid interface produced a 4.1 K change in Tj,max, which returned to within 0.3 K of baseline upon restoring inflation layers; this confirmed the necessity of wall-normal refinement and provided a negative control.

5. Resolution Studies

Spatial refinement:
- Three systematically refined meshes were generated with identical topology: 2.1M, 4.7M, and 8.9M control volumes. Inflation layers: 18, 26, and 34 layers respectively, first cell height set to target y+ ≈ 0.6 in all cases. Area-averaged y+ values were 0.9 (coarse), 0.7 (medium), and 0.5 (fine).
- At the highest load case (die peak 95 W, 1.2 L/min, 40 C inlet), Tj,max was 162.8 K (coarse), 161.1 K (medium), and 160.6 K (fine). Using the GCI approach with observed order p ≈ 1.92, the estimated mesh uncertainty on Tj,max at the medium grid is 2.1 K (1.3%). Similar GCI percentages on baseplate temperature gradients were 1.8–2.5%.

Temporal aspects:
- The model is steady. A transient check with pseudo-transient stepping (fixed CFL) confirmed that steady solutions are unique for the explored operating points; no hysteresis observed. A short (2 s) transient initialization was performed and then stopped when residual criteria and monitors converged.

Iterative convergence:
- At each operating point, residuals were driven below 1e-6 and Tj,max stabilized within 0.05 K over an additional 300 iterations. Mass flow imbalances <0.01%; energy closure within 0.5% as stated above.

6. Inputs: Pedigree, Ranges, and Control

- Thermal losses: Derived from inverter switching models (PLECS) calibrated on the dynamometer at 20 kHz; uncertainty ±5% (95% CI) per die, with known spatial nonuniformity captured by a 3 × 3 heat map per die. For validation runs, electrical power was metered at the DC bus and phase currents; thermal loss fraction derived accounting for magnetic core and copper losses in the inductor downstream (separate temperature logs used to subtract non-module heat).

- Coolant conditions: Bench loop with Coriolis meter (±0.5% of reading) and 4-wire RTDs (±0.15 C). Inlet total temperature uncertainty ±0.2 C; flow rate uncertainty ±0.6% including calibration drift.

- TIM properties: Vendor datasheet 6 ± 0.5 W/m-K; independent guarded-hot-plate test measured 5.7–6.3 W/m-K at 25–60 C. Thickness measured at assembly (78 ± 11 µm, 1σ) via feeler gauge at four corners.

- Material properties: Temperature-dependent tables for Al and Cu from ASM; AlN conductivity taken as 170 W/m-K at 25 C with −0.3%/K slope per vendor.

- Emissivity for IR validation: 0.92 ± 0.02 for black-painted copper; emissivity set in camera and cross-checked with a reference blackbody tape.

All inputs were tracked in a Git repository (GitLab CE 16.5). Each scenario is a parameter file with a SHA-256 hash. Only calibrated inputs were allowed to change between validation and prediction stages with explicit change logs.

7. Experimental Program and Comparison

Test bench:
- Custom loop with gear pump, 12 L reservoir, plate heat exchanger to maintain inlet temperature. Three operating points for each inlet temperature (25, 35, 45 C) and three flow rates (0.8, 1.2, 1.6 L/min) yielded a 3 × 3 matrix. Die losses set at 40, 70, and 95 W per die, with identical spatial loss maps to those used in the model.

Instrumentation:
- Six T-type thermocouples embedded in the copper baseplate (0.5 mm below the TIM contact surface), two upstream and two downstream of the hottest die cluster, and two at corners; accuracy ±0.2 C post-calibration. IR camera (FLIR A655sc) monitored top copper and die copper caps; emissivity calibrated. Pressure drop across module logged to estimate channel Reynolds number and corroborate flow maldistribution model.

Calibration and holdout:
- A single scalar multiplier on the TIM effective conductivity (k_eff_mult) was fitted using the mid-range condition (35 C, 1.2 L/min, 70 W/die) to account for assembly-specific contact imperfections. The best-fit multiplier was 0.93. No other parameters were tuned. All other data were treated as holdout.

Agreement metrics:
- Across 26 holdout points, the mean absolute error in Tj,max was 3.4 K; the 95th percentile error was 7.9 K; the maximum error was 8.6 K. The slope of predicted vs measured Tj,max was 0.98 with intercept 1.2 K (R^2 = 0.96). No observable drift with inlet temperature.
- Baseplate thermocouples: mean absolute error 1.8 K; worst case 4.1 K at the lowest flow rate due to slightly higher measured gradient near a bend—consistent with small-scale roughness not present in the CAD.
- Spatial fields: IR maps showed hot-spot locations consistent within 2–3 mm of model predictions; the model tended to smear the peak slightly, which is expected under RANS with transitional turbulence.

8. Quantified Uncertainty and Sensitivity

Propagation:
- Major sources included die loss uncertainty (±5%), TIM thickness (±14 µm, 2σ), TIM conductivity (±0.5 W/m-K, 2σ), coolant flow rate (±0.6%), inlet temperature (±0.2 C), and numerical resolution (from Section 5). We treated die losses as correlated within each die but uncorrelated between dies in different clusters; other inputs independent.
- Latin Hypercube Sampling with 200 samples was performed at two representative operating points (low and high flow) for inlet temperatures 25 C and 45 C. Each sample run used the medium mesh; numerical uncertainty from spatial discretization was added as a separate random variable (normal, σ = 1.2 K based on GCI).

Results:
- At the high-load, mid-flow point (70 W/die, 1.2 L/min, 35 C), the combined 95% bound on Tj,max was +8.7/−7.9 K relative to the nominal prediction; mean shift was +0.6 K (slight positive bias due to lognormal TIM thickness).
- Across the envelope, the 95% upper bound for Tj,max prediction error (model vs. truth) including validation residuals, input uncertainty, and numerical effects was ≤9.6 K.

Sensitivity:
- Using the Morris method with eight trajectories, the rank order of influence on Tj,max was:
  1) TIM thickness (mu* = 5.8 K/10 µm),
  2) coolant flow rate (mu* = −3.3 K per 0.1 L/min),
  3) die loss amplitude (mu* = 2.1 K per 5 W),
  4) TIM conductivity (mu* = −1.4 K per 0.5 W/m-K),
  5) inlet temperature (mu* ≈ 1.0 K per 1 C),
  6) numerical grid (treated as noise level, mu* ≈ 0.5 K).
- Interaction terms were modest; the only notable nonlinearity was between flow rate and die loss at the highest loads, but within single-phase range.

9. Coverage of Evidence vs. Intended Use

- Operating space: Validation covered 9 of the 9 combinations of inlet temperature and flow rate, and three loss levels per combination; this spans the intended use envelope without extrapolation.
- Physics similarity: Reynolds numbers, Prandtl numbers, and material property ranges matched those expected in vehicle operation; the bench used the same coolant blend and fittings as the vehicle loop.
- Geometry fidelity: The cold-plate used for validation is an off-the-line sample from the supplier (Lot CP-2026-03); metrology scans showed ±10 µm deviations on channel width and ±15 µm on depth relative to CAD. These small deviations are not represented in the CAD and are a plausible contributor to the ∼4 K worst-case baseplate error.

10. Software and Process Quality

- Configuration control: All case files, parameter sets, postprocessing scripts (Python 3.10), and results are under GitLab with protected branches. Tags identify baseline runs used in this report. Containerized pre/post environment (Apptainer, Ubuntu 22.04 image) captured dependencies and exact versions.
- Solver environment: Fluent 2024 R1 build 20240215, double precision, run on HPE ProLiant DL380 (2× Intel Xeon Silver 4316) with 256 GB RAM; parallel runs with 24 processes; decomposition kept fluid–solid interfaces intact to avoid interpolation across partitions.
- Reproducibility: A new analyst re-ran two randomly selected validation points from scratch using the repository instructions and reproduced Tj,max within 0.2 K and wall-clock time within 5%.
- Peer review: The thermal group at the drivetrain division, not involved in design of the cold plate, performed an internal review of the model setup, scripts, and this assessment. Comments and resolutions are tracked in Issues #143–#155 in the repository.

11. Assumptions and Model Form Choices

- Single-phase coolant behavior: No boiling expected within the stated envelope; peak wall temperature margin to saturation >25 K at lowest flow and highest die loss per Sieder–Tate estimates.
- Transitional turbulence treatment: Given Re range straddling laminar–transitional regimes, the transitional SST model was used; sensitivity to laminar modeling at Re < 1000 showed <0.7 K change in Tj,max.
- TIM homogeneity: TIM modeled as homogeneous anisotropic slab; roughness and clamping pressure variations abstracted into the k_eff_mult parameter. The single multiplier was fitted at a mid-range condition and then held fixed.
- Radiation: Included only from the top copper surface to ambient; enclosure effects negligible (view factor <0.05 to surrounding housing at 35 C).

12. Credibility Synthesis

- Evidence strength: The breadth of validation (26 holdout points), low bias (slope 0.98, intercept 1.2 K), and bounded worst-case error (8.6 K) support use for design screening within the envelope. Numerical errors were quantified and small relative to the acceptance threshold. Input uncertainties were systematically propagated, and the 95% bound on Tj,max stays within 10 K for representative conditions.
- Weaknesses: The need to fit a single TIM multiplier indicates sensitivity to assembly-specific factors; however, cross-validation suggests this is a stable representation of the as-built condition. Micro-geometry deviations in the serpentine bends are not in the CAD and can affect local heat transfer—these effects presented in baseplate thermocouple residuals are within acceptable limits for the decision at hand.
- Independence: Peer review by a separate team and the use of production hardware for validation reduce confirmation bias risks. All modifications between calibration and predictions are documented.

13. Limitations and Non-coverage

- The model is not suitable for assessing short-duration transients (<15 s), thermal cycling-induced fatigue, or die temperature overshoot during current surges; time-accurate conjugate simulations would be required.
- Boiling inception, vapor entrapment, or coolant aeration are out of scope. The current evidence does not support predictions above 120 W/die at 45 C inlet with flows below 0.8 L/min; those conditions risk two-phase onset.
- The turbulence approach is RANS-based; near-wall heat transfer in separated micro-bends may be underpredicted by 5–10% compared to scale-resolving methods. The current validation shows this is bounded in our geometry.
- Manufacturing variability beyond the measured lot CP-2026-03 is not captured; geometry tolerances larger than ±20 µm in the channel cross-section could degrade accuracy.

14. Traceability and Records

- Model files: repo tag coldplate-cht-v1.7, commit 7f9a2c1. Parameter sets under params/2026Q3/.
- Validation data: raw logs and processed CSVs under data/bench-CP2026-03/. Instrument calibrations are archived in docs/calibration/2026Q2/.
- Review records: issues #143–#155 closed with reviewer approvals.
- Run manifests: runmanifests/ contain case hashes, solver settings, and machine info for each simulation.

15. Conclusion and Decision

The assembled evidence indicates the conjugate heat transfer model predicts Tj,max and baseplate gradients within the bounds required for design screening across the intended operating envelope. Agreement with independent bench data is strong, numerical errors are small relative to the decision threshold, and uncertainties from inputs and assembly are characterized and propagated.

Decision:
- By the Thermal Design Authority (Lead: M. R. Patel), the model identified as coldplate-cht-v1.7 is accepted for predicting:
  - peak junction temperature and baseplate temperature distribution for steady operating points with coolant inlet 20–50 C, flow 0.8–1.6 L/min, and die losses 30–95 W per die,
  - supporting design screening and thermal margin assessment with a 15 K margin target,
  subject to the following conditions: use the calibrated TIM multiplier k_eff_mult = 0.93 for builds assembled under the same process controls as CP-2026-03; flag any changes in TIM material or assembly torque for re-assessment.

- The model is not approved for evaluating transient warm-up behavior, two-phase conditions, or coolant aeration scenarios; separate analysis and/or testing are required for those cases.

Authorization: Approved on 2026-08-05 by M. R. Patel (Thermal Design Authority) and countersigned by L. Chen (Drivetrain Validation Lead).
